title: Reading user-selected files: File and Blob
summary: The browser wraps a user-selected file in a File (a Blob with a name), and hands you .text(), .arrayBuffer() and .stream() — Promises instead of the legacy FileReader callbacks.

examples.title: Size guards, text(), and streaming a big file

annotations.note: File extends Blob: the bytes plus name/type/lastModified. You never get a path — the browser gives you the content, not the filesystem.
Check size before reading. .text() loads everything; a 2 GB "CSV" without this guard freezes the tab — the trap Go's os.ReadFile has too.
.text() returns a Promise: await it. The legacy FileReader and its onload callbacks are unnecessary for whole-file reads.
.stream() is a ReadableStream: constant memory for big files, the browser twin of bufio.Scanner. getReader() + read() yields chunks.

use_cases: CSV/JSON import in a UI before upload (validate client-side first)
Generating exports: new Blob([...]) + object URL + click an <a download>
strengths: .text()/.arrayBuffer()/.stream() are one-liners with no callback plumbing
.stream() handles files far larger than memory
File/Blob work in drag-and-drop, input elements and clipboard identically
weaknesses: No path access: you cannot re-read the same file later without asking the user again
.text() decodes as UTF-8 by default; other encodings need TextDecoder with an explicit label
Legacy Safari-era code and many tutorials still use FileReader callbacks

pitfalls.title: Reading whole files without a size guard
pitfalls.detail: One .text() on a huge file locks the tab. Guard with file.size, stream with .stream() beyond a threshold.

pitfalls.title: Assuming File.name is a safe path
pitfalls.detail: It's a name, possibly '../evil'. If you send it anywhere, treat it as untrusted input.

pitfalls.title: Mixing up Blob and File types in APIs
pitfalls.detail: Accept Blob in helpers; File is a subtype, so both work.

options: Display it, but treat it as untrusted data — never a path
Nothing; reject all files with slashes
quiz.why: The name is display metadata only; the browser gives you content, not filesystem access.

quiz.q: You need to read a possibly-500 MB log in the browser. Which API?
quiz.why: .text() materializes the whole content; .stream() yields chunks with constant memory.

body:
## Concept

`<input type="file">` (or drag-and-drop) gives you `FileList` of `File` objects. A `File` is
a `Blob` — immutable bytes plus metadata — with `.text()`, `.arrayBuffer()`, `.stream()` and
`.slice()`. Whole-file reads are one awaited call; big files stream chunk by chunk.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Go: `os.ReadFile` vs `bufio.Scanner` maps exactly onto `.text()` vs `.stream()` — but the
  browser starts from the user's choice, not a path.
- Node: `fs.readFile` takes paths; the browser deliberately never does (security).
- C: no FILE* here. The sandbox is the point: the page sees only what the user picked.

## Design notes

Treat client-side reading as *pre-validation before upload*: parse, check, then send only
what's needed. The browser sandbox (no paths, user-initiated reads) is worth internalizing —
it's the same least-privilege thinking as the SQL playground role, which owns only sandbox
objects. The TraceLite import step (Phase 7) wires this lesson's pattern to a Go server.
